title: Reflexive verbs
description: Talk about your daily routine and about what people do to each other with verbs like se lever and se parler.

guide.summary: Reflexive verbs put the action back on the subject: se lever, se coucher, s’appeler. The work is in the little pronoun in front of the verb: it changes with the subject, it shrinks before a vowel, and it has a fixed place in a negative sentence.

sections.title: What a reflexive verb is
sections.text: A reflexive verb carries a pronoun that points back at the subject: the person does the action to themselves. The same verb without that pronoun acts on somebody or something else.

rows: je lave la voiture (I wash the car)
je lève la main (I raise my hand)
je me couche (I go to bed)
je couche les enfants (I put the children to bed)
je m’appelle Marie (my name is Marie)

examples.fr: Je me réveille à sept heures.

watch: Drop the pronoun and the meaning changes: je lave means I wash something else.
English hides the reflexive: “I get up”, “my name is”, “I have fun”, “I hurry” are all reflexive in French.

sections.title: Which pronoun goes with which subject?
sections.text: The reflexive pronoun repeats the subject. Learn the six forms and the rest follows.
steps: Find the subject: who is doing it?
Take that person’s row and use the pronoun written there.
Put the pronoun between the subject and the verb, then give the verb the ending of the same person.

examples.en: Do you hurry in the morning?

watch: Se belongs to il, elle, on, ils and elles only: it is the dictionary form, not an all-purpose pronoun.
The first and second person plural write the word twice: nous nous levons, vous vous levez. That is correct.
On behaves like il: on se couche tard.

sections.title: Me, te and se before a vowel
sections.text: Me, te and se lose their e in front of a vowel or a silent h, and an apostrophe takes its place. Nous and vous never change.

columns: Before a vowel or silent h

steps: Look at the first letter of the verb that follows.
Vowel or silent h: cut the e of me, te or se and glue the rest on with an apostrophe.
Consonant: keep the pronoun whole. Nous and vous stay whole in every case.

examples.en: We are having a good time.

watch: The h of habiller and habiter is silent, so it counts as a vowel: il s’habille.
Never “se amusent” or “te amuses”: the apostrophe is compulsory.
The apostrophe replaces the e and leaves no space: m’appelle, not m’ appelle.

sections.title: Where do ne and pas go?
sections.text: Ne and pas wrap around the pronoun and the verb together. The pronoun never leaves its verb.
steps: Keep the pronoun and the conjugated verb glued together.
Put ne in front of that pair and pas straight after the verb.
Everything else (tôt, le soir, avant minuit) stays at the end.

examples.fr: Je ne me lève pas tôt.
Elle ne s’habille pas en noir.

watch: Not “je me ne lève pas”: the pronoun comes after ne, not before it.
Not “ne se pas réveille”: pas comes after the verb, never between pronoun and verb.
In speech people drop ne (je me lève pas); written French keeps it.

sections.title: After aller, vouloir, pouvoir, devoir
sections.text: Only the first verb is conjugated. The reflexive verb stays in the infinitive, and its pronoun still matches the subject and sits right in front of it.
steps: Conjugate the first verb (aller, vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, aimer) for the subject.
Leave the reflexive verb in the infinitive.
Take the pronoun for the subject and put it right before that infinitive.

examples.en: You can get dressed on your own.

watch: Do not keep the dictionary se: the pronoun changes with the subject even before an infinitive.
The pronoun travels with the infinitive, never before the first verb: not “je me vais coucher”.
Moi, toi, lui and the other stressed pronouns never take this place.

sections.title: Saying “each other”
sections.text: With a plural subject the same pronoun can mean each other instead of oneself. The sentence tells you which.

rows: nous nous voyons le samedi (we see each other)
vous vous téléphonez souvent (you phone each other)
ils se parlent, elles s’écrivent (they talk / write to each other)

steps: Check that the subject is plural: two people or more.
Use the reflexive pronoun that matches that subject.
Add nothing for “each other”: the pronoun already says it.

examples.en: Luc and Léa love each other.

examples.fr: Mon frère et moi, nous nous téléphonons le soir.
examples.en: My brother and I phone each other in the evening.

watch: There is no word-for-word “each other” in French: never “chaque autre”.
Mes amis et moi, mon frère et moi are first person plural subjects, so the pronoun is not the third-person one.

sections.title: Body parts take le, la, les
sections.text: When a reflexive verb acts on a part of the body, French puts a definite article in front of it. The reflexive pronoun already says whose it is.
steps: Use the reflexive verb with the pronoun of the subject.
Give the body part a definite article, chosen by its gender and number.
Leave out mon, ton, son, mes, tes, ses: the owner is named once, by the pronoun.
watch: Not “je me lave mes mains”: French never names the owner twice.
Hands, teeth, feet and cheveux are plural in French, so they take a plural article.
Without the reflexive verb the possessive comes back: je lave ses cheveux (I wash her hair).

sections.title: Spelling changes: lève, promène, appelle
sections.text: Some -er verbs change their stem when the ending is silent (je, tu, il/elle/on, ils/elles) and keep the plain stem when the ending is pronounced (nous, vous).

columns: Silent ending: je, tu, il, ils
rows: je me lève, ils se lèvent
nous nous levons, vous vous levez
je me promène, ils se promènent
nous nous promenons, vous vous promenez
nous nous appelons, vous vous appelez

steps: Write the present ending for the subject first.
Ask whether that ending is silent (-e, -es, -ent) or pronounced (-ons, -ez).
Silent: change the stem (è for lever and promener, double l for appeler). Pronounced: keep the stem of the infinitive.

examples.fr: Je me lève, nous nous levons.
examples.en: I get up, we get up.

watch: The accent and the double l never show up with nous or vous.
Appeler keeps its two p’s everywhere: only the l doubles.
Se promener follows se lever: ils se promènent, but vous vous promenez.

steps: Find the subject of the sentence.
Take the reflexive pronoun on that person’s row.
Check that the verb ending belongs to the same person.
Look at the letter right after the blank.
Vowel or silent h: cut the e of me, te or se and add an apostrophe.
Consonant, or a first or second person plural pronoun: keep the whole form.
Find the conjugated verb and keep its pronoun directly in front of it.
Put ne before that pronoun.
Put pas directly after the verb, before the rest of the sentence.
Spot the two verbs: the first is conjugated, the second stays in the infinitive.
Choose the pronoun that matches the subject, not the dictionary se.
Place that pronoun immediately before the infinitive.
Identify the plural subject: the pronoun matches it, as always.
Let the reflexive pronoun carry “each other” and add no extra words.
Give the verb the ending of that plural subject.
Keep the reflexive pronoun in front of the verb.
Give the body part a definite article, chosen by gender and number.
Remove any possessive: the pronoun already names the owner.
Write the present ending for the subject.
Decide whether that ending is silent or pronounced.
Change the stem only when the ending is silent.

exercises.hint: The reflexive pronoun always matches the subject.
exercises.feedback: Se is only for il, elle, on, ils and elles.
exercises.explanation: Nous nous couchons: with nous, the reflexive pronoun is nous too.

mistakes.why: Se and s’ belong to il, elle, on, ils and elles. The subject here is first person plural, and its reflexive pronoun simply repeats the subject word; s’ would also need a vowel sound after it.

exercises.hint: Mes parents means ils. Réveillent starts with a consonant.
exercises.feedback: Only one option is a reflexive pronoun that fits ils before a consonant.
exercises.explanation: Ils se réveillent: the pronoun for ils is se, and it does not elide before a consonant.

mistakes.why: That is the shortened form, used only in front of a vowel or a silent h. Réveillent begins with a consonant, so the pronoun keeps its e.
Leur is a possessive or an indirect object pronoun (to them). It points at other people, not back at the subject, so it cannot be the reflexive pronoun.

exercises.hint: Match the pronoun to the subject vous.
exercises.feedback: Se is only for the third person. Look at the subject again.
exercises.explanation: Vous vous dépêchez: with vous, the reflexive pronoun is also vous.

mistakes.why: Se is the third person pronoun, for il, elle, on, ils and elles. The subject here is the person being spoken to, who has another pronoun.
Te goes with tu, one person addressed informally. This subject is the polite or plural form, which uses its own matching pronoun.
Nous is the pronoun for a first person plural subject (we). Here the subject is the people spoken to, not the speaker.

exercises.hint: Put the pronoun that matches tu before the verb.
exercises.feedback: The reflexive pronoun for tu is not se.
exercises.explanation: Tu te couches: te matches tu, and coucher takes -es with tu.

mistakes.why: Se is the dictionary pronoun, kept for il, elle, on, ils and elles. With tu the pronoun has to change with the subject.
That verb form is the il/elle one. An -er verb adds an s for tu.
The ending -ez belongs to vous. The subject given is the informal singular.
Me belongs to je, and the bare infinitive is the dictionary form. The task asks for the present tense with the subject tu, pronoun included.

exercises.hint: Check that the pronoun matches the subject.
exercises.feedback: Se is for il, elle, on, ils and elles only.
exercises.explanation: Tu te couches: the reflexive pronoun for tu is te.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence exactly as it was: it still uses the third person pronoun after tu. Change the pronoun so it matches the subject.
The pronoun is fixed but the verb lost its ending: with tu an -er verb ends in -es.
Changing the subject, or deleting the pronoun, answers a different question. The subject tu must stay and the verb still needs a reflexive pronoun.

exercises.hint: Use se coucher. The pronoun matches the subject.
exercises.feedback: With nous, the reflexive pronoun is nous; with on, it is se.
exercises.explanation: Nous nous couchons tard, or with on: on se couche tard.

mistakes.why: The verb ending fits the subject but the pronoun was left in its dictionary form, which only works for il, elle, on, ils and elles.
Without a reflexive pronoun, coucher means putting someone else to bed. Going to bed yourself needs the pronoun.
With the subject on, the pronoun is the third person one; as written, this says that somebody else puts us to bed.
That is word-for-word English. French says it with the reflexive verb se coucher.

exercises.hint: Appelle starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Me cannot stand before a vowel, and se does not match je.
exercises.explanation: Je m’appelle: me becomes m’ before a vowel.

mistakes.why: The pronoun is the right one for je, but it cannot keep its e in front of a vowel: the e drops and an apostrophe replaces it.
Se belongs to il, elle, on, ils and elles, not to je, and it would also have to shorten before appelle.

exercises.hint: The h of habiller is silent, so habille sounds as if it starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Se loses its e before a vowel sound.
exercises.explanation: Il s’habille: se becomes s’ before a vowel or a silent h.

mistakes.why: That is the full form, used before a consonant. The h of habille is silent, so the word sounds as if it starts with a vowel and the e has to go.
Me is the pronoun for je. The subject here is il, which uses the third person pronoun.
The e that drops must be replaced by an apostrophe; a bare consonant is not a French word.
That is the direct object pronoun (him, it). A reflexive verb needs a pronoun that points back at the subject.

exercises.hint: Amuses starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Te cannot stay whole before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Tu t’amuses: te becomes t’ before a vowel.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the pronoun still keeps its e in front of a vowel.
The apostrophe is right, but the verb lost its ending: with tu an -er verb ends in -es.
S’ is the third person form. The subject is tu, so the shortened pronoun must be the tu one.

exercises.hint: The pronoun for je is me. What happens before a silent h?
exercises.feedback: Me is elided before a silent h.
exercises.explanation: Je m’habille: me becomes m’ before the silent h of habille.

mistakes.why: Habille starts with a silent h, which counts as a vowel: the pronoun cannot keep its e in front of it.
That pronoun comes from the dictionary form and belongs to il, elle, on, ils and elles. With je it starts with another letter.
The ending -es goes with tu. With je an -er verb ends in -e.
That is the infinitive. The task asks for the present tense, so the verb needs the je ending.

alternatives.message: That is understandable but stiff. This exercise asks for the reflexive verb: Elle s’appelle Léa.

exercises.hint: French says she calls herself. Appelle starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Use the reflexive verb with elle, and elide the pronoun before the vowel.
exercises.explanation: Elle s’appelle Léa: s’appeler with elle, s’ before a vowel, and a double l.

mistakes.why: The pronoun has to lose its e in front of the vowel of appelle and take an apostrophe instead.
The verb is built on appeler, with two p’s; this version drops one of them.
This verb doubles its l in front of a silent ending, so a single l is wrong here.
Il is a male subject. The English says her, so the subject must be the feminine one.

exercises.source: The children have fun in the garden.
answers: Les enfants s’amusent dans le jardin.
exercises.hint: Amusent starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: One tile keeps se whole before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Les enfants s’amusent: se becomes s’ before a vowel.

answers: Les enfants se amusent dans le jardin.
mistakes.why: That tile keeps the e of the pronoun in front of a vowel. Amusent begins with a, so the e must drop and an apostrophe takes its place.

exercises.hint: Change the pronoun and the verb ending. Does nous ever elide?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun for nous is nous, and it never becomes an apostrophe form.
exercises.explanation: Nous nous amusons: nous never elides, even before a vowel.

mistakes.why: The first person plural pronoun never shortens, even before a vowel, and this version has lost it altogether.
The ending -ent belongs to ils and elles. A first person plural subject takes -ons.
S’ belongs to il, elle, on, ils and elles. When the subject changes, the reflexive pronoun changes with it.
That verb form goes with il or elle. The new subject needs its own ending.

exercises.instruction: Make it negative in standard written French.
answers: Je ne me lève pas tôt.

alternatives.message: That is common in speech. The written form also needs ne before me.

exercises.hint: Ne goes before the reflexive pronoun, pas after the verb.
exercises.feedback: The pronoun stays attached to the verb, inside the negation.
exercises.explanation: Je ne me lève pas: ne comes before me, pas comes after lève.

answers: Je me ne lève pas tôt.
mistakes.why: The first word of the negation comes before the reflexive pronoun; the pronoun has to stay glued to its verb.
The reflexive pronoun disappeared, and without it lever means to lift something else.

answers: Je me lève ne pas tôt.
mistakes.why: Ne and pas do not sit together after the verb: they wrap around the pronoun and the verb.

exercises.instruction: Make it negative in standard written French.
answers: Elle ne s’habille pas en noir.

alternatives.message: That is common in speech. The written form also needs ne before s’.

exercises.hint: Ne goes before the pronoun s’.
exercises.feedback: Do not separate s’ from the verb, and do not forget ne.
exercises.explanation: Elle ne s’habille pas: ne before s’, pas after habille.

answers: Elle s’ne habille pas en noir.
mistakes.why: The shortened pronoun cannot be cut off from its verb; the first word of the negation goes in front of the pronoun.

answers: Elle ne habille pas en noir.
mistakes.why: The reflexive pronoun is gone, so the sentence says she dresses somebody else.

answers: Elle ne s’habille en noir pas.
mistakes.why: Pas goes straight after the conjugated verb, not at the end of the sentence.

exercises.hint: The reflexive pronoun stays right before the verb.
exercises.feedback: Ne and pas surround the pronoun and the verb together.
exercises.explanation: Il ne se réveille pas: ne + pronoun + verb + pas.

mistakes.why: This puts the reflexive pronoun before the negation. The negation word comes first, straight after the subject.
Pas comes after the conjugated verb, never between the pronoun and the verb: those two stay side by side.
The reflexive pronoun is never left at the end. It sits in front of its verb, inside the negation.

exercises.source: We aren’t going for a walk this evening.
answers: Nous ne nous promenons pas ce soir.
exercises.hint: Start with the subject, then ne, then the reflexive pronoun.
exercises.feedback: The reflexive pronoun sits between ne and the verb.
exercises.explanation: Nous ne nous promenons pas: subject, ne, pronoun, verb, pas.

answers: Nous nous ne promenons pas ce soir.
mistakes.why: The negation word comes before the reflexive pronoun, which must stay directly in front of the verb.

answers: Nous ne promenons pas ce soir.
mistakes.why: Without the reflexive pronoun, promener means walking someone else, a dog for instance.

answers: Nous ne nous pas promenons ce soir.
mistakes.why: Pas belongs after the conjugated verb, not in front of it.

exercises.source: Je me ne couche pas avant minuit.
answers: Je ne me couche pas avant minuit.
exercises.hint: Which comes first after the subject: ne or the reflexive pronoun?
exercises.feedback: The pronoun must stay directly before the verb.
exercises.explanation: Je ne me couche pas: ne comes before me, and me stays next to couche.

answers: Je me ne couche pas avant minuit.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the pronoun still splits the negation. It belongs right next to the verb.

answers: Je me couche ne pas avant minuit.
mistakes.why: Ne never sits after the verb: it goes in front of the pronoun, and pas after the verb.

answers: Je ne couche pas avant minuit.
mistakes.why: Deleting the reflexive pronoun is not the fix: it changes the meaning to putting someone else to bed. Only the word order was wrong.

answers: Ils ne se lèvent pas tôt.

alternatives.message: That is common in speech. The written form also needs ne before se.

exercises.hint: Use se lever. Watch the accent in the ils form.
exercises.feedback: Ne goes before se, pas after the verb.
exercises.explanation: Ils ne se lèvent pas tôt: ne + se + lèvent + pas. Lever takes è when the ending is silent.

answers: Ils ne se lève pas tôt.
mistakes.why: That verb form is for one person. A plural subject needs the -ent ending.
The reflexive pronoun is missing, and without it the verb means lifting something.

answers: Ils se ne lèvent pas tôt.
mistakes.why: The first word of the negation goes before the reflexive pronoun, not after it.

answers: Elles ne se lèvent pas tôt.
mistakes.why: Elles is the feminine subject. The English marks the group as masculine.

exercises.hint: Two words are missing before the verb: the first part of the negation and the reflexive pronoun.
exercises.feedback: Check the order: the pronoun stays next to the verb.
exercises.explanation: Elle ne se promène pas: ne, then se, then the verb.

mistakes.why: Wrong order: the reflexive pronoun must stay directly in front of the verb, so the negation word has to come first.
That gives the negation but loses the reflexive pronoun, which se promener cannot do without.
The pronoun only drops its e before a vowel or a silent h. Promène starts with a p.
That is the negation of être. The verb here is promener, and it still needs its reflexive pronoun.

exercises.hint: After aller, the infinitive keeps a pronoun that matches the subject.
exercises.feedback: The subject is je, so the pronoun is not se. Moi cannot stand before a verb.
exercises.explanation: Je vais me coucher: the pronoun matches je, even though coucher is an infinitive.

mistakes.why: Se is the dictionary pronoun of the verb. Even in front of an infinitive it changes to match the subject, and the subject here is je.
Moi is a stressed pronoun, used alone or after a preposition. It never stands in front of a verb as the reflexive pronoun.

exercises.hint: The subject is elles. Promener starts with a consonant.
exercises.feedback: A subject pronoun cannot replace the reflexive pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Elles aiment se promener: se matches elles and stays whole before a consonant.

mistakes.why: The e drops only before a vowel or a silent h. Promener begins with a consonant, so the pronoun stays whole.
That is a subject pronoun, and it is already the subject of the sentence. The infinitive needs a reflexive pronoun of its own.

exercises.hint: The pronoun matches the subject, not the infinitive.
exercises.feedback: Se is the dictionary form. Here the subject is tu.
exercises.explanation: Tu dois te dépêcher: the infinitive keeps a pronoun that matches tu.

mistakes.why: Se is the dictionary form, kept for il, elle, on, ils and elles. After devoir the pronoun still matches the subject, which is tu.
The pronoun shortens only before a vowel or a silent h. Dépêcher begins with d.
Toi is a stressed pronoun: it follows an imperative or a preposition, never an ordinary verb it belongs to.
Vous goes with the polite or plural subject. The subject given here is the informal singular.

exercises.source: Nous voulons se promener au bord de la mer.
answers: Nous voulons nous promener au bord de la mer.
exercises.hint: Se is the dictionary form of the pronoun. Who is going for the walk?
exercises.feedback: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject nous.
exercises.explanation: Nous voulons nous promener: after vouloir, the pronoun still matches nous.

answers: Nous voulons se promener au bord de la mer.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the infinitive still carries the dictionary pronoun, which does not match the subject.

answers: Nous voulons se promenons au bord de la mer.
Nous voulons nous promenons au bord de la mer.
mistakes.why: After vouloir the second verb stays in the infinitive; conjugating it twice is not the fix.

answers: Nous nous voulons promener au bord de la mer.
mistakes.why: The reflexive pronoun belongs to the second verb, so it stays in front of the infinitive, not in front of vouloir.

exercises.source: I’m going to go to bed.
exercises.hint: Use aller plus se coucher. The pronoun matches je.
exercises.feedback: Do not keep se: the pronoun must match the subject.
exercises.explanation: Je vais me coucher: aller + infinitive, with me matching je. Je vais aller me coucher is also correct.

mistakes.why: The dictionary pronoun is only for il, elle, on, ils and elles. In a sentence it changes to match the subject, here je.
Without a reflexive pronoun, coucher means putting someone else to bed.
The pronoun belongs to the infinitive, not to aller: it sits directly before the verb it goes with.
After aller the second verb stays in the infinitive; this one is a conjugated present.

exercises.source: You must get up at six o’clock. (formal)
answers: Vous devez vous lever à six heures.
exercises.hint: After devoir, the infinitive keeps a pronoun that matches the subject.
exercises.feedback: One tile is the dictionary form of the pronoun. It does not match vous.
exercises.explanation: Vous devez vous lever: the pronoun vous matches the subject and sits before the infinitive.

answers: Vous devez se lever à six heures.
mistakes.why: That tile is the dictionary pronoun, kept for il, elle, on, ils and elles. Before the infinitive the pronoun still has to match the subject.

answers: Vous vous devez lever à six heures.
mistakes.why: The pronoun goes with the infinitive it belongs to, directly in front of it, not in front of devoir.

answers: Vous devez lever à six heures.
mistakes.why: With no reflexive pronoun, lever means lifting something or getting somebody else up.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the sentence starting with Tu peux.
exercises.hint: The reflexive verb becomes an infinitive after pouvoir. Keep the pronoun that matches tu.
exercises.feedback: Keep t’ before the infinitive, and use the infinitive form of the verb.
exercises.explanation: Tu peux t’habiller seul: t’ matches tu and stays before the infinitive.

mistakes.why: After pouvoir the second verb stays in the infinitive; this one is still conjugated for tu.
S’ is the third person pronoun. In front of the infinitive the pronoun still matches the subject tu.
Dropping the pronoun makes the verb mean dressing somebody else; the reflexive pronoun must stay before the infinitive.
The pronoun belongs to the second verb and stays right in front of it, not before pouvoir.

exercises.instruction: Choose the pronoun that means each other.
exercises.source: Mes amis et moi, nous ____ voyons le samedi.
exercises.hint: The subject is nous. The pronoun always matches it.
exercises.feedback: Se does not go with nous.
exercises.explanation: Nous nous voyons: with nous, the reciprocal pronoun is nous (we see each other).

mistakes.why: Se and s’ work only with il, elle, on, ils and elles. Mes amis et moi is a first person plural subject, so the pronoun repeats that subject word.

exercises.hint: Each other is expressed by the reflexive pronoun.
exercises.feedback: No extra words are needed for each other: the pronoun does the job.
exercises.explanation: Ils se parlent: se means each other with a plural subject.

mistakes.why: French has no word-for-word “each other” in this position; the meaning is carried by the reflexive pronoun in front of the verb.
The verb must agree with a plural subject, so it needs the -ent ending.
The pronoun loses its e only before a vowel or a silent h; parlent starts with p, so it keeps its full form.
Elles is the feminine subject. The English marks the group as masculine.

exercises.instruction: Write the pronoun that means each other.
exercises.hint: Paul et Julie means ils. Écrivent starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Se loses its e before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Paul et Julie s’écrivent: se means each other and becomes s’ before a vowel.

mistakes.why: Écrivent begins with a vowel, so the pronoun cannot keep its e in front of it.
That pronoun goes with a first person plural subject. Paul et Julie are two other people, a third person plural subject.
Leur is an indirect object pronoun (to them): it points at other people, not back at the subject.
The dropped e must be replaced by an apostrophe; a bare letter is not a word.

exercises.instruction: Combine into one sentence with a reciprocal verb.
exercises.source: Luc aime Léa. Léa aime Luc.

exercises.feedback: The verb needs a reflexive pronoun, elided before the vowel.
exercises.explanation: Luc et Léa s’aiment: se means each other and becomes s’ before aiment.

mistakes.why: Aiment starts with a vowel, so the pronoun must drop its e and take an apostrophe.
Two people are the subject, so the verb needs its plural ending.
Without a reciprocal pronoun the verb has no object, and nothing says the feeling goes both ways.
That pronoun and that ending belong to a first person plural subject. Here the subject is two other people.

exercises.source: We see each other after school.
exercises.hint: Each other is the reflexive pronoun that matches nous.
exercises.feedback: One tile only works with il, elle, on, ils or elles.
exercises.explanation: Nous nous voyons: the second nous means each other.

mistakes.why: That tile is the third person pronoun, for il, elle, on, ils and elles. A first person plural subject repeats its own subject word.
Without the reciprocal pronoun the verb has no object: seeing each other needs the pronoun in front of the verb.

exercises.source: Mon frère et moi, nous se téléphonons le soir.
answers: Mon frère et moi, nous nous téléphonons le soir.
exercises.hint: The subject is nous. Does the pronoun match?
exercises.feedback: Se does not go with nous.
exercises.explanation: Nous nous téléphonons: the reciprocal pronoun matches nous.

answers: Mon frère et moi, nous se téléphonons le soir.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: the pronoun is still the third person one while the subject is first person plural.
